Tumor tissue demonstrated loss of MSH6 protein expression by staining; MSI testing was negative. Germline MSH6 R1331X mutation detected.

- No additional physical exam findings, treatment plan, or follow-up instructions were documented in the provided dialogue.

### Proposed Diagnosis ###
1. Endometrial carcinoma (endometrioid-type most likely) – Lynch syndrome–associated with germline MSH6 R1331X and tumor loss of MSH6 (most likely cause of current bleeding)
2. Endometrial carcinoma of a non-endometrioid histology (serous/clear cell/mixed) – less likely but possible pending full pathologic subtype
3. Atypical endometrial hyperplasia (precursor lesion/coexisting lesion) – possible concomitant lesion but less likely given tumor on D&C
4. Cervical neoplasm (cervical cancer or cervical polyp) – less likely given uterine tumor sampling but should be excluded on exam/Pap/colposcopy
5. Uterine sarcoma (eg, leiomyosarcoma or endometrial stromal sarcoma) – rare, less likely than endometrial adenocarcinoma but remains a differential for abnormal bleeding until full histology/staging is available

[THOUGHT]
The proposed primary diagnosis—endometrial carcinoma, likely Lynch (MSH6)-associated—is well aligned with the new data: D&C retrieved tumor tissue, tumor IHC shows loss of MSH6 protein, and germline MSH6 R1331X mutation was detected. Loss of MSH6 with a pathogenic germline MSH6 variant strongly supports a diagnosis of an MMR-deficient endometrial malignancy. However, the case summary does not explicitly provide the formal histopathology report (definitive statement of carcinoma vs atypical hyperplasia, histologic subtype, grade, depth of myometrial invasion, lymphovascular invasion), nor any staging imaging or clinical pelvic/cervical exam findings. MSI was negative — which can occur with MSH6 defects — but this discordance should be documented and reconciled. Important red flags or critical elements missing: confirmation of malignant histology and subtype/grade, assessment for extent of disease (pelvic MRI or CT), cervical exam/Pap/colposcopy to exclude cervical source, documentation of hemodynamic status relative to ongoing bleeding, and workup for Lynch-associated synchronous/interval cancers (colonoscopy). Genetic counseling and cascade testing documentation are also not described.

[DECISION]
INCOMPLETE

[FEEDBACK]
Required critical information/tests to make a defensible, conclusive diagnosis and safe next steps (prioritize in this order):
1. Formal surgical pathology report from the D&C: definitive diagnosis (carcinoma vs atypical hyperplasia), histologic subtype (endometrioid vs serous/clear cell), grade, depth of myometrial invasion (if available), and presence/absence of lymphovascular space invasion.
2. Pelvic/cervical clinical exam findings and speculum exam documentation (to exclude cervical source of bleeding); obtain Pap/HPV testing or colposcopy if indicated.
3. Cross-sectional imaging for local and regional staging (pelvic MRI preferred for myometrial and cervical involvement; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis if higher-stage disease suspected).
4. Clarify MSI/IHC discordance in pathology report (MSH6 loss with MSI negative) and confirm IHC panel results for all MMR proteins.
5. Consult/notification of gynecologic oncology for management planning (surgical staging vs other therapies).
6. Preoperative labs and assessments if surgery planned: CA-125 (adjunct), repeat CBC if bleeding persists, coagulation studies as indicated.
7. Genetic counseling documentation and plan for Lynch syndrome management: colonoscopy screening, cascade testing for first-degree relatives, and tailored surveillance.
8. Additional clinical details: amount/duration of bleeding, physical stability, contraception/anticoagulant history (if still unknown), and family cancer history.

Once the formal pathology report and staging workup are available and gynecologic oncology assessment documented, the diagnosis of Lynch-associated endometrial carcinoma can be considered confirmed and management planned.
